item.title: Re: What is the evidence for school smartphone bans?
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor, I write in response to Matthew Sadlier's rapid response. With respect, Professor Sadlier's argument relies far more on analogy and anecdote than on the actual evidence about school phone policies. First, comparing smartphones to tobacco is rhetorically striking but scientifically bankrupt. item.title: Re: Pneumonia: “Alarming” rise in emergency admissions in England, data show
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor Excellent piece. I think a few factors play a role as mentioned above. But I would add anecdotal evidence here which is professionals' hesitancy to prescribe antibiotics for MDR fears installed during the past few years or so. It’s a balance after all. item.title: Re: Machine learning based screening of potential paper mill publications in cancer research: methodological and cross sectional study
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor, Scancar and colleagues use machine-learning screening of titles and abstracts to estimate the prevalence of paper-mill activity in cancer research [1]. The study is useful in that it assigns scale to a problem usually discussed qualitatively. The durability of the reported prevalence estimates seems however questionable and uncertain. item.title: Is "recent" a habit or a choice? The role of linguistic sensitivity
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor, Díez-Vidal and Arribas provide a fascinating analysis of the term "recent" in biomedical literature (1). While they describe the term as a "flexible rhetorical device", I suggest that the variation in citation lag might be explained by a hidden variable: the author's linguistic sensitivity. item.title: To cut the £3.6bn negligence bill, we must price risk before we price failure
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor The Public Accounts Committee’s warning that clinical negligence costs have risen to around £3.6bn a year should not be read only as a legal or accounting problem. It signals a systems failure: we are willing to pay an unlimited price for failure, yet repeatedly refuse to price risk upfront [1]. item.title: The importance of statistical reasoning in vaccination-related legal disputes
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor The recently published BMJ article highlights the critical role of robust statistical reasoning in medical misconduct cases and the serious consequences of its misuse in legal settings (1).
